title: Record keeping, digital and numeracy skills
blurb: Write records that are contemporaneous, accurate, attributable and secure, on paper and on screen.
question: At the end of a busy shift, a nurse realises she did not document a patient's fall that happened six hours earlier. How should she record it now?

teach.body: Records are how the team knows what has happened, what risks exist and what to do next. Code 10 requires clear and accurate records relevant to your practice. Plain English: if it is not written down clearly, the next nurse cannot act on it, and nobody can show the care was given. Records cover paper and electronic notes, charts, care plans and other documents in your scope of practice.

head: Standard
Requirement
rows: Complete at the time or as soon as possible; note if written later
Identify risks or problems and the steps taken
Accurate, no falsification; act if others falsify
Attributed, dated, timed; no unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation
Collect, treat and store data and research findings appropriately

teach.body: Write records at the time or as soon as possible after the event. If you write some time later, make that clear: record the time you are writing and the time the event happened. Never alter, backdate or falsify an entry. If you discover that someone else has falsified a record, you must take immediate and appropriate action (Code 10.3).

teach.h: Worked scenario: Staff Nurse Lena on a respiratory ward
teach.body: Mr Shah, 79, slipped at 14:00; Lena checked him, called the doctor and started neurological observations, but did not write it up. At 20:00 she writes a late entry headed with the time of writing, stating the fall occurred at 14:00, what she observed, who she informed and the actions taken, without guesses such as 'probably confused'. She signs it and completes an incident report.

rows.label: Cause
values: 'Found on floor at 14:00, said he slipped'

teach.caption: Record what you saw, heard, measured and did, not opinions or guesses.
UK GDPR principles include accuracy, data minimisation and integrity and confidentiality (security).

teach.h: Numeracy and digital skills for safe practice (P1.15)
items: Record observations and doses with the correct units, written clearly.
Check calculations and chart totals such as fluid balance before acting on them.
Use electronic systems as designed; do not work around alerts without good reason.
Analyse and share digital information only with those who need it for care (Annexe A 1.10).

teach.text: A late entry is acceptable; a BACKDATED entry is not. Write the actual time you are writing, and state when the event happened. Never make it look as if it was written at the time.

items: Write at the time or as soon as possible; mark late entries clearly (10.1).
Accurate, no falsification; act if others falsify (10.3).
Attributed, dated, timed; no unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation (10.4).
Keep records secure; never share log-ins; access on a need-to-know basis (10.5).

summary: You can now write records that meet Code 10: contemporaneous, accurate, attributed, dated and timed, free of speculation and kept secure. You can also handle late entries honestly and keep digital records safe.

A.q: When should a nurse complete a record of care she has given?
options: Before handover at the end of the shift
Before the next consultant ward round
Within 24 hours of the event occurring
At the time or as soon as possible after
A.why: Code 10.1: complete all records at the time or as soon as possible after an event, recording if the notes are written some time after.

whyNot.0: Waiting until the end of the shift risks missed or inaccurate information.
whyNot.1: Ward round timing is not the standard set by the Code.
whyNot.2: The Code sets no 24-hour window; it asks for as soon as possible.

options: '14:30 15/03: refused lunch, said she felt nauseous. J. Ade RN'
'Pt difficult again today re meals, NFA at present, will review'
'Seems low in mood and is probably missing her family at home'
'Lunch not taken today, see previous note for details'
A.why: Code 10.4: entries must be attributed, dated and timed, clearly written and free of unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation.

whyNot.1: This uses jargon and abbreviations and gives an opinion, not facts.
whyNot.2: This is speculation about her mood and its cause.
whyNot.3: It is not dated, timed or attributed, and gives no detail.

A.q: A colleague asks to use your smartcard to update a care plan because hers is not working. What should you do?
options: Lend it, staying beside her as she types
Log in and enter her notes for her
Decline and help her get access sorted
Lend it and check her entries afterwards
A.why: Entries must be attributed to the person making them (Code 10.4) and records kept secure (10.5). Sharing log-ins makes entries inaccurate and breaches security.

whyNot.0: Supervising her does not change that entries would be wrongly attributed to you.
whyNot.1: Entering her care under your name misattributes the record.
whyNot.3: Checking afterwards does not fix the false attribution.

B.q: A nurse realises at 21:00 that she forgot to record a blood glucose of 3.2 mmol/L treated at 16:00. How should she document it?
options: Write it in the 16:00 slot as if on time
Write a late entry stating both times
Tell the night nurse and leave it unrecorded
Record it on a sticky note on the chart
B.why: Code 10.1: complete records as soon as possible after the event, recording if the notes are written some time after. A clearly marked late entry is honest and accurate.

whyNot.0: Making it look contemporaneous misrepresents the record (Code 10.3).
whyNot.2: A verbal handover does not replace the record.
whyNot.3: Loose notes are not secure or part of the formal record.

B.q: A healthcare assistant has filled in four-hourly observation charts for times when the observations were not taken. What must the nurse do?
options: Correct the charts herself so they are complete
Leave it, as the patient's observations were stable
Take immediate and appropriate action
Discuss it with the assistant at the next appraisal
B.why: Code 10.3: take immediate and appropriate action if you become aware that someone has not kept to the requirement for accurate records without falsification, such as escalating to the nurse in charge.

whyNot.0: Altering the charts herself would be further falsification.
whyNot.1: Falsification is serious whatever the clinical outcome.
whyNot.3: Waiting for an appraisal is not immediate action.

B.q: Which UK GDPR principle is breached when a nurse leaves a patient record open on an unattended ward computer?
options: Integrity and confidentiality
Purpose limitation
Storage limitation
Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
B.why: The integrity and confidentiality (security) principle requires appropriate security for personal data; Code 10.5 asks nurses to keep records secure.

whyNot.1: Purpose limitation concerns using data only for the purpose it was collected.
whyNot.2: Storage limitation concerns not keeping data longer than needed.
whyNot.3: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency concern the basis for and openness of processing; the direct breach here is security.

C.q: A nurse documents 'Patient aggressive, needs sedating' after a distressed man shouted at staff. What is the main problem with this entry?
options: It is not countersigned by a doctor
It is too short to be useful
It should be written in the incident log
It gives opinion rather than observed facts
C.why: Code 10.4 asks for entries without speculation. The record should state what was seen and heard, what was done and the outcome.

whyNot.0: Nursing entries do not need a doctor's countersignature.
whyNot.1: Length is not the issue; the content is judgemental and vague.
whyNot.2: An incident report may also be needed, but the clinical record must still be factual.

C.q: A nurse is curious about a celebrity admitted to another ward and looks at their electronic record. Which Caldicott principle is breached?
options: Comply with the law
Access on a strict need-to-know basis
Inform patients how their data is used
Use the minimum necessary information
C.why: Caldicott principle 4: access to confidential information should be on a strict need-to-know basis. She has no care role for this patient.

whyNot.0: Unlawful access may follow, but the specific principle is need-to-know access.
whyNot.2: Informing patients about data use is a separate principle.
whyNot.3: Minimum necessary concerns how much is used for a justified purpose; here there is no purpose.

C.q: A nurse adds up a fluid balance chart and gets a positive balance of 3,500 mL in 24 hours for a patient with heart failure. What should she do first?
options: Record the total and continue the plan
Stop his IV fluids until the doctor reviews
Recheck the calculation, then escalate
Wait until the next day's total to compare
C.why: Numeracy for safe practice (P1.15) means checking calculations before acting, then escalating a concerning finding promptly (Code 10.2, 13.2).

whyNot.0: A large positive balance in heart failure needs action, not just recording.
whyNot.1: Changing fluids without a review and a checked total may harm the patient.
whyNot.3: Waiting a day delays escalation of a possible overload.

reteach.title: Write it for a stranger
reteach.question: Could a nurse who has never met this patient act safely on your entry alone?

blocks.body: Imagine your entry is read by an agency nurse, a coroner or the patient. They need to know when it happened, who wrote it, what was observed, what was done and what to do next. If any of those is missing, or if it contains an opinion you cannot back with facts, rewrite it.

blocks.text: Abbreviations are not banned, but UNNECESSARY ones are (Code 10.4). If a reader could misread it, write it in full.

explain.body: Write records at the time or as soon as possible, noting when an entry is written some time after the event.

test.q: Which phrase best describes how a late entry should be written?
options: Clearly marked with the time it was written
Placed in the slot where the event occurred
Kept separately until the manager approves it
Written by the nurse in charge instead
test.why: Code 10.1: record if the notes are written some time after the event, so the actual time of writing must be shown.

whyNot.1: Placing it in the earlier slot hides that it is late.
whyNot.2: No approval is needed to write a late entry.
whyNot.3: The nurse who gave the care should write it.

explain.body: Complete records accurately without falsification. If someone else falsifies records, take immediate and appropriate action.

test.q: Which Code standard requires records to be completed accurately and without falsification?
test.why: Code 10.3: complete all records accurately and without falsification.

whyNot.2: 10.6 is about data and research findings.

explain.body: Attribute entries to yourself, date and time them, and avoid unnecessary abbreviations, jargon and speculation.

test.q: Which feature is required by Code 10.4 for every record entry?
options: A countersignature from a colleague
Attribution to the person making it
A copy sent to the patient's GP
Use of approved abbreviations
test.why: Code 10.4: attribute any entries you make to yourself, clearly written, dated and timed.

whyNot.2: Copying to a GP is not a Code 10.4 requirement.
whyNot.3: The Code asks you to avoid unnecessary abbreviations, not to use them.

explain.body: Keep paper and electronic records secure. Do not share log-ins, lock screens, and access only what you need for care.

test.q: A nurse takes a photo of a handover sheet on her personal phone to remember her jobs. Which Code standard does this most directly breach?
options: 10.1 timely records
10.2 identifying risks
10.5 keeping records secure
10.4 avoiding jargon
test.why: Code 10.5: take all steps to make sure records are kept securely. Copying patient information to a personal device breaches this.

whyNot.1: Risk identification is not the issue.
